source: Piper et al. (2003) The BrainIT group: concept and core dataset definition
text: This is the minimum minute by minute monitoring data required for inclusion in the BrainIT Database and include: Heart Rate (specifying source: ECG or Pulse Oximetry), Respiration Rate (sources: impedance plethmography or ventilator), Mean Arterial Pressure, mean ICP, Pulse Oximetry (SaO2) and Temperature (sources: rectal=oesophageal= bladder=skin.) However, additional variables: Central Venous Pressure (CVP), EtCO2, SjO2, TCD, PbrO2, Brain Temperature, Microdialysis. . . will also be included in the database if they are monitored, in a given patient, as part of their usual clinical management.

classes.label: Heart Rate
classes.evidence: Heart Rate (specifying source: ECG or Pulse Oximetry)

classes.label: Respiration Rate
classes.evidence: Respiration Rate (sources: impedance plethmography or ventilator)

source: Piper et al. (2003) The BrainIT group: concept and core dataset definition
text: Intensive care management information. Types of data include: GCS scores, pupil scores, ventilation settings, sedation levels, fluid input and output, nutrition, use of vasopressors, antibiotics. Routine blood gases and daily laboratory values will also be recorded – Biochemistry (Na, K+, Glucose), Haematology (Haemoglobin, White Cell Count, Haematocrit).

source: Piper et al. (2003) The BrainIT group: concept and core dataset definition
text: Secondary insults such as intracranial hypertension, systemic hypotension, arterial hypotension, jugular venous desaturation, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) are adverse physiological events that occur frequently in head injured patients despite baseline intensive care management.

classes.label: Condition
classes.evidence: adverse physiological events that occur frequently in head injured patients

source: Piper et al. (2003) The BrainIT group: concept and core dataset definition
text: Therapy data is divided into two categories: baseline therapy covering routine ICU management delivered to all patients (ventilation settings, sedation levels, fluid input and output, nutrition, vasopressors, antibiotics), and secondary insult therapy covering non-surgical medical management specifically given to treat secondary insults, with assigned therapy targets (e.g. arterial pressors targeting systemic hypotension or reduced CPP secondary to raised ICP).

classes.label: Baseline Therapy
classes.evidence: baseline therapy covering routine ICU management

classes.label: Secondary Insult Therapy
classes.evidence: secondary insult therapy covering non-surgical medical management

classes.label: Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP)
classes.evidence: reduced CPP secondary to raised ICP

source: Piper et al. (2003) The BrainIT group: concept and core dataset definition
text: ICU management data also covers nursing activities that are annotated: routine nursing care (eye/mouth care, ET tube suction, bed care), physiotherapy sessions, bedside interventions (line insertion/renewal, transducer calibration, x-ray), and patient transport (to and from Theatre or CT-Scan). The patient outcome is measured using the Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOSe) at 6 months.

classes.label: Routine Nursing Care
classes.evidence: routine nursing care (eye/mouth care, ET tube suction, bed care)

classes.label: Bedside Intervention
classes.evidence: bedside interventions (line insertion/renewal, transducer calibration, x-ray)

classes.label: Patient Transport
classes.evidence: patient transport (to and from Theatre or CT-Scan)

classes.evidence: Extended Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOSe) at 6 months

source: Moss et al. (2013) Trusting Intensive Care Unit (ICU) Medical Data
text: For the TBI domain, we used data consisting of 37 patients, 595,439 distinct timepoints, 4,467,949 observations for 14 parameters. In both domains, data is collected every minute. For the Medical Disorders rule, we created specific queries for hypotension and hypertension; and for the Treatments rule, queries for effects of noradrenaline and adrenaline.

source: Piper et al. (2010) The BrainIT collaborative network: EC feasibility study results
text: A set of therapy categories have been defined with some associated therapy type detail. For every therapy given an intended target must also be given (e.g. mannitol for raised ICP). These include: Sedation, Analgesia, Paralysis, Volume expansion, Inotropes, Anti-hypertensives, Anti-pyretics, Hypothermia, Steroids, Cerebral vasoconstriction, Osmotics (mannitol), Barbiturates.

source: Piper et al. (2010) The BrainIT collaborative network: EC feasibility study results
text: Vital monitoring data are bedside monitoring data which are collected at regular intervals with a minimum sampling rate of once per minute. The parameters monitored include: BP (blood pressure: mmHg; systolic, diastolic, mean), ICP (intracranial pressure: mmHg; mean), CPP (cerebral perfusion pressure: mmHg; mean), HRT (heart rate: bpm), SaO2 (arterial oxygen saturation: %; pulse oximetry), Tc (core temperature: degrees C).

classes.label: Monitoring Data
classes.evidence: Vital monitoring data are bedside monitoring data

classes.label: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)
classes.evidence: BP (blood pressure: mmHg; systolic, diastolic, mean)

source: Shaw et al. (2024) Exploration of the relationship between PbtO2 and ICP
text: Clinical management of this population is focused on minimising any secondary injury, such as ischemia or raised intracranial pressure (ICP). To help quantify the current pathophysiology and provide information on changing injury status, a variety of vital signs monitoring modalities are used concurrently in neuro-intensive care units. Monitoring of ICP is indicated in the current neurotrauma guidelines for patients with TBI. Metabolic activity, disease severity and mortality is related to the partial pressure of brain tissue oxygen (PbtO2).

classes.label: Secondary Insult
classes.evidence: secondary injury, such as ischemia or raised intracranial pressure

classes.label: PbrO2
classes.evidence: partial pressure of brain tissue oxygen (PbtO2)

source: Shaw et al. (2024) Exploration of the relationship between PbtO2 and ICP
text: The currently proposed treatment protocols using a combined PbtO2 and ICP monitoring strategy are still using singular cut-offs, 20 mmHg for PbtO2 and 22 mmHg for ICP, for these parameters. There is also a known non-linear effect of PbtO2 on cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), which is the net pressure differential driving cerebral blood flow across the cerebrovascular bed and directly influenced by ICP.

source: Georgatzis et al. (2016) Artefact in Physiological Data Collected from Patients with Brain Injury
text: Arterial hypotension and increased intracranial pressure (ICP) are secondary insults that are associated with poor outcome in patients suffering traumatic brain injury (TBI). Through the acquisition of high-frequency physiological data and using predictive modelling techniques there is now the potential to predict these secondary insults with the possibility of intervening before the event.

classes.label: Secondary Insult
classes.evidence: secondary insults that are associated with poor outcome

source: Georgatzis et al. (2016) Artefact in Physiological Data Collected from Patients with Brain Injury
text: Hypotensive events were classified as either mean ABP (ABPm) less than 70 mmHg or systolic ABP (ABPs) less than 90 mmHg. For an event to be valid it had to remain below the threshold for at least 5 min. Also included in the BrainIT data set are a series of annotations of nursing and medical interventions such as blood sampling, transducer calibration, endotracheal suction and patient turning.

source: Decraene et al. (2023) Decompressive craniectomy as a second/third-tier intervention in TBI
text: First-tier treatments include head elevation, neuromuscular paralysis, analgesia, continued sedation, normocapnia and normothermia. Second-tier treatments include deepening of sedation, cerebrospinal fluid drainage, moderate hypocapnia, and administration of hyperosmolar molecules. When despite these interventions ICP remained unacceptably high, decompressive craniectomy was chosen as a next step, with or without first having applied third-tier medical therapy with barbiturates (thiopental).

classes.label: Secondary Insult Treatment
classes.evidence: decompressive craniectomy was chosen as a next step

source: Decraene et al. (2023) Decompressive craniectomy as a second/third-tier intervention in TBI
text: Mean intracranial pressure (ICP), mean cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) and mean pressure reactivity index (PRx) were calculated six hours before and seven days after decompressive craniectomy for each patient. Also, the median percentage of monitoring time with ICP greater than 20 mmHg, ICP greater than 25 mmHg, CPP less than 60 mmHg were determined. Patient outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended (GOSe) at six months post-injury.

classes.label: GOSe Outcome
classes.evidence: Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended (GOSe) at six months post-injury

source: Donald et al. (2012) Trigger Characteristics of EUSIG-Defined Hypotensive Events
text: Hypotension is a recognized secondary insult after traumatic brain injury (TBI). The definition of hypotension used is systolic pressure less than 90 mmHg or mean arterial pressure less than 70 mmHg for a holddown of 5 minutes. Several authors have shown that significant periods of arterial hypotension consistently relate to clinical outcome.

classes.label: Hypotension
classes.evidence: Hypotension is a recognized secondary insult

classes.label: Secondary Insult
classes.evidence: secondary insult after traumatic brain injury

classes.label: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)
classes.evidence: mean arterial pressure less than 70 mmHg

source: Güiza et al. (2015) Visualizing the Pressure and Time Burden of Intracranial Hypertension
text: Intracranial pressure (ICP) monitoring was introduced as a monitoring tool for severe TBI. The recommended treatment threshold for ICP-lowering therapies is 20 mmHg. An increased ICP is an independent risk factor for mortality, and the total burden of ICP derangements, calculated as the area under the ICP curve above 20 mmHg, is an independent predictor of worse outcome in adults and children.

classes.label: Monitoring Data
classes.evidence: ICP monitoring was introduced as a monitoring tool

classes.label: Intracranial Hypertension
classes.evidence: increased ICP is an independent risk factor

source: Güiza et al. (2015) Visualizing the Pressure and Time Burden of Intracranial Hypertension
text: Data collection in both cohorts included baseline risk factors (age, gender, admission GCS, admission pupil reactivity), minute-by-minute ICP and mean arterial blood pressure (MAP) monitoring data, and Glasgow Outcome Score (GOS) at 6 months. The low-frequency autoregulation index (LAx) is computed as a moving minute-by-minute correlation of previous values of ICP and MAP.

source: Stell et al. (2018) Automated Measurement of Adherence to TBI Guidelines
text: Using a combination of physiological and treatment information from neurological ICU data-sets, adherence to traumatic brain injury (TBI) guidelines on hypotension, intracranial pressure (ICP) and cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is calculated automatically. Aggressive attempts to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure above 70 mmHg with fluids and pressors should be avoided because of the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

source: Depreitere et al. (2018) Cerebral Perfusion Pressure Variability
text: The recommendation for targeting cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) in the Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines on the management of severe traumatic brain injury has changed from keeping CPP above 70 mmHg to 50-70 mmHg. The change to recommending lower CPP was mainly inspired by the non-beneficial effect of keeping CPP above 70 mmHg by administering high doses of vasopressors. CPP variability was independent of intracranial pressure, and hence was also reflected in mean arterial pressure (MAP) variability.

classes.label: Derived Parameter
classes.evidence: CPP variability was independent of intracranial pressure

source: Donald et al. (2012) Trigger Characteristics of EUSIG-Defined Hypotensive Events
text: The Edinburgh University Secondary Insult Grades (EUSIG) system classifies a hypotensive event as systolic blood pressure (BPs) less than 90 mmHg or mean arterial pressure (BPm) less than 70 mmHg with a holddown period of 5 minutes. The distinction between BPs and BPm is important because the trigger characteristics and clinical significance of these event types differ.

classes.label: EUSIG Grade
classes.evidence: Edinburgh University Secondary Insult Grades (EUSIG) system

classes.label: Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP)
classes.evidence: systolic blood pressure (BPs) less than 90 mmHg

classes.label: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)
classes.evidence: mean arterial pressure (BPm) less than 70 mmHg

source: Georgatzis et al. (2016) Artefact in Physiological Data Collected from Patients with Brain Injury
text: A significant proportion of the physiological signals acquired from brain-injured patients in neuro-ICU are corrupted by artefact. Sources of artefact include nursing interventions such as endotracheal suctioning, patient turning and transducer calibration. An ECG-based heart rate signal may be less susceptible to certain artefact types compared with pulse oximetry-derived heart rate.

classes.label: Artefact
classes.evidence: signals acquired from brain-injured patients in neuro-ICU are corrupted by artefact

classes.label: Nursing Intervention
classes.evidence: nursing interventions such as endotracheal suctioning

source: Decraene et al. (2023) Decompressive craniectomy as a second/third-tier intervention in TBI
text: Decompressive craniectomy (DC) was performed as a hemicraniectomy or bifrontal craniectomy. Cranioplasty was subsequently performed using the original bone flap. Therapy intensity level (TIL basic) was recorded for each patient to quantify the intensity of ICP-directed treatment. First-tier treatments include head elevation (30 degrees), neuromuscular paralysis, analgesia, and sedation. Injury mechanisms included fall, road traffic accident, assault and sport injuries. In-hospital mortality was 18%.

classes.label: Injury Mechanism
classes.evidence: Injury mechanisms included fall, road traffic accident, assault

source: Guiza et al. (2015) Visualizing the Pressure and Time Burden of Intracranial Hypertension
text: The pressure-time dose of intracranial hypertension, defined as the area under the ICP curve above a threshold, is an independent predictor of 6-month mortality. Cerebrovascular autoregulation status, assessed via the pressure reactivity index (PRx), modulates the relationship between ICP burden and outcome. Patients with intact autoregulation tolerate higher ICP doses than those with impaired autoregulation.

classes.label: Pressure-Time Dose
classes.evidence: pressure-time dose of intracranial hypertension, defined as the area under the ICP curve

classes.label: Outcome
classes.evidence: relationship between ICP burden and outcome
